title: Act III, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Juliet impatiently waits for night and Romeo. The Nurse arrives lamenting; Juliet thinks Romeo is dead, then learns Tybalt is dead and Romeo banished. She briefly condemns Romeo, then defends him. The Nurse promises to bring Romeo to her.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act III, Scene II,” how does Shakespeare show Juliet hears the news? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act III, Scene II, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Juliet hears the news? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act III, Scene II develops the idea of Juliet hears the news. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and diction / vocabulary shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act III, Scene II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of Juliet hears the news. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act III, Scene II suggests about Juliet hears the news. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's irony and diction / vocabulary), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses irony in Act III, Scene II to complicate the reader's understanding of Juliet hears the news. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act III, Scene II within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Juliet hears the news responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act III, Scene II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Juliet hears the news follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene II and its treatment of Juliet hears the news. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's irony and diction / vocabulary, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene II as evidence for a larger claim about Juliet hears the news in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene II as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Juliet hears the news. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

themesAndDevelopment.development: Juliet chooses husband over cousin: "My husband lives, that Tybalt would have slain."

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “would whip you to the west, / And bring in cloudy night immediately. / Spread thy close curtain, love-performing night, / That runaways’ eyes may” (Act III, Scene II, Juliet (speech 1)).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: would whip you to the west, / And bring in cloudy night immediately. / Spread thy close curtain, love-performing night, / That runaways’ eyes may

symbolsAndMotifs.name: fate and the stars
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: From "star-cross'd" in the Prologue to Romeo's "I defy you, stars," the lovers feel steered by fortune, while the plot shows human choices and accidents. In this scene: “shall die, / Take him and cut him out in little stars, / And he will make the face of heaven so fine / That” (Act III, Scene II, Juliet (speech 1)).

On imagery: "Come, night; come, Romeo; come, thou day in night." Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
